title: Seleucid Mesopotamia
subtitle: 331–141 BC · The Greek Kings on the Tigris — the Wars of the Successors, Seleucia the New Royal City, the Cuneiform Twilight and the Coming of the Parthians

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Seleucus winning Babylon back in the war of the successors, the founding of Seleucia-on-the-Tigris, Antiochus I as restorer of the temples, Antiochus III's march east and Antiochus IV's Greek Babylon, and the Parthian conquest of 141

entries.label: Seleucus I — the satrap who won a kingdom
entries.hint: Seleucus was given the satrapy of Babylon in the carve-up of 320, driven out by Antigonus in 315, and came back with a small force on a day the Babylonians long remembered — the first year of what became the Seleucid Era. He held the province through a hard four-year war, took the title of king around 305, ceded the far eastern lands to Chandragupta for five hundred war-elephants, and by his murder in 281 ruled from the Aegean to the Hindu Kush.
entries.note: The Chronicle of the Diadochi (BCHP 3); Appian, 'Syriaca' 54–57; Diodorus Siculus XIX.90–92 on the return of 311.

entries.label: Antiochus I — the restorer of the temples
entries.hint: Antiochus had governed the eastern half of the empire from Babylon as his father's co-king for fifteen years before he inherited it. In 268 he laid the foundations of Ezida at Borsippa in person and had the act recorded on a clay cylinder in Akkadian, in the old royal style — the last document of its kind. He also founded and settled Greek cities, and fought a long war to hold Syria against the Ptolemies.
entries.note: The Antiochus Cylinder (Borsippa, 268 BC); Paul-Alain Beaulieu in 'The Oxford Handbook of Cuneiform Culture' (2011).

entries.label: Antiochus II and Seleucus II — the middle reigns
entries.hint: Under Antiochus II and his son Seleucus II the dynasty turned on itself. A disputed marriage set off the Third Syrian War in 246: Ptolemy III's army marched up the Euphrates and into Babylon, and for a year the city was fought over street by street while a Seleucid garrison held the citadel. Seleucus II recovered the province but never the initiative, and lost the far east to the Parthians and Bactrians.
entries.note: The Ptolemy III Chronicle (BCHP 11); Justin, 'Epitome' XXVII; the 'Gurob papyrus' on the Egyptian march.

entries.label: Antiochus III the Great — the march east and the Roman check
entries.hint: Antiochus III put down a revolt that had seized Seleucia, then spent seven years marching to Bactria and India and back, recovering the appearance of empire. He turned west, collided with Rome, and was beaten at Magnesia in 190; the Treaty of Apamea took Anatolia and imposed a crushing indemnity. He died in 187 trying to plunder a temple in Elymais to help pay it.
entries.note: Polybius V.40–56 (Molon) and XXI (Apamea); Diodorus XXVIII–XXIX; the death in Elymais in Strabo XVI.1.18.

entries.label: Antiochus IV Epiphanes — the Greek city in Babylon
entries.hint: Antiochus IV gave Babylon a Greek constitution — a citizen body, a council, magistrates and a theatre — turning the old temple-city into a self-governing polis alongside its priesthood. The same policy of forced Hellenisation in Jerusalem produced the Maccabean revolt. He died in 164 on campaign in the Iranian highlands; a Babylonian record notes the news reaching the city.
entries.note: The Astronomical Diaries for 175–164 BC (Sachs & Hunger); the Babylonian King List of the Hellenistic Period; 1 Maccabees 1; 6.

entries.label: The last Seleucid decades and the loss of the land
entries.hint: After Antiochus IV the dynasty spent itself in succession wars fought in Syria, and Babylonia was governed at a distance by strategoi who could expect little help. When the Parthian king Mithridates I came down the Tigris in 141 there was no field army to stop him. Demetrius II marched east to recover the province in 138, was defeated and taken prisoner, and spent ten years as an Arsacid son-in-law.
entries.note: The Astronomical Diary for 141 BC, which dates by 'Arsaces the king'; Justin XXXVI.1 and XXXVIII.9; Josephus, 'Antiquities' XIII.

entries.label: The satrap, the strategos and the royal city
entries.hint: Babylonia was run for the king by a satrap, later titled strategos, seated at Seleucia — the eastern half of the empire's administrative capital, where the mint struck and the tribute was gathered. Below him a network of officers, most with Greek titles, oversaw the districts, the garrisons and the royal land. The king himself was normally at Antioch, on the far side of the Syrian desert.
entries.note: Getzel Cohen, 'The Hellenistic Settlements in the East' (2013); Laurent Capdetrey, 'Le pouvoir séleucide' (2007).

entries.label: The citizen body and the temple assembly
entries.hint: In the old cities the crown left the running of civic life to two bodies: the temple assembly — the šatammu of the Esagila and the kiništu council of priests and prebend-holders — and, in Babylon after Antiochus IV, a Greek-style citizen corporation, the politai, who appear in the Astronomical Diaries under an Akkadian version of the word. A royal overseer sat above both.
entries.note: R. J. van der Spek, 'The Hellenistic Diaries and the Political History of Babylon' (2000); the puliṭē / politai in the Diaries.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Babylonian War of 311–309 and the devastation the chronicles record, the elephant campaigns, the Ptolemaic sack of 246, the revolt of Molon at Seleucia, and Mithridates I's annexation of the land

entries.label: The Babylonian War and the devastation of the land
entries.hint: When Seleucus came back in 311, Antigonus sent first his son Demetrius and then his whole army to take the province from him. The fighting ran for two years across the countryside; a Babylonian chronicle records 'weeping and mourning in the land', crops burnt and cities plundered, before Seleucus won a night battle and Antigonus withdrew for good. It fixed Babylonia as Seleucid.
entries.note: The Chronicle of the Diadochi (BCHP 3); Diodorus Siculus XIX.100.

entries.label: Ipsus and the ownership of the east
entries.hint: The four other successors combined against Antigonus and destroyed him at Ipsus in Phrygia in 301; Seleucus's Indian elephants decided the day. The battle was fought a thousand kilometres away, but it settled that Babylonia and the whole Asian core would be ruled from a single Seleucid throne rather than contested between warlords — the political fact that made Seleucia possible.

entries.label: The Ptolemaic army in Babylon
entries.hint: In the Third Syrian War Ptolemy III drove up through Syria and into Mesopotamia. A Babylonian chronicle records his troops fighting inside Babylon in 245, people killed in the streets, and a Seleucid garrison holding out in the royal fortress until relief came. It was the deepest a Ptolemaic army ever reached, and the last time Egypt threatened the Seleucid heartland.
entries.note: The Ptolemy III Chronicle (BCHP 11); the 'Adulis inscription' (OGIS 54) for the Egyptian account.

entries.label: The revolt of Molon at Seleucia
entries.hint: Molon, satrap of Media, rebelled against the young Antiochus III, crossed the Tigris, took Seleucia and the lowland cities, and struck his own royal coinage. Antiochus came east in person, caught Molon's army near the river, and won when part of it changed sides; Molon killed himself and his body was displayed. The king then crossed into Babylonia and sacrificed at the Esagila.

entries.label: The anabasis and the Roman indemnity
entries.hint: Antiochus III's seven-year march recovered tribute and treaties from Armenia to India and won him the title 'the Great'. Then Rome broke him at Magnesia in 190 and the Treaty of Apamea in 188 stripped Anatolia and imposed fifteen thousand talents of silver. The debt sent him and later his son to rob the temples of the eastern hills, where he was killed in 187.
entries.note: Polybius XXI.42–45 (Apamea); Livy XXXVII–XXXVIII; Strabo XVI.1.18.

entries.label: Mithridates I takes Babylonia
entries.hint: The Parthian king Mithridates I came down from Media and entered Seleucia in 141; within months the Diaries were dating documents by 'Arsaces the king'. Demetrius II's counter-attack in 138 ended in his capture. A last Seleucid effort under Antiochus VII briefly retook the land in 130 and collapsed when he was killed in battle in 129. After that Babylonia was Parthian for good.
entries.note: The Astronomical Diaries for 141 and 130–129 BC; Justin XXXVI.1, XXXVIII.9–10, XLII.1.
